title: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
summary: Why the best learning rate drifts with width under standard parametrization, how muP rescales init, multipliers and per-layer learning rates to stop the drift, and how to apply and verify muTransfer.
outcomes: Explain why optimal hyperparameters shift with width under the standard parametrization
Explain why weight updates need a 1/fan_in factor while random init needs only 1/sqrt(fan_in)
Compute muP learning rates, init scales and multipliers for a target width from a tuned proxy
Decide which hyperparameters can be tuned on a proxy and which cannot
Verify a muP implementation with a coordinate check and spot common bugs

lessons.title: Why the best learning rate drifts as models get wider

blocks.md:
Tuning hyperparameters (HPs) such as learning rate, initialization scale and output multipliers takes many full training runs. At billions of parameters that is unaffordable, so teams tune a small model and guess. The guess is usually wrong in the standard setup.

In Tensor Programs V (Yang, Hu et al., 2022) a 2-hidden-layer MLP trained on CIFAR-10 with SGD in the **standard parametrization** saw its best learning rate shift by roughly an order of magnitude as the hidden width grew from 256 to 8192. Using the narrow model's best learning rate on the wide one gave very bad results, if not divergence. Transformers trained with Adam showed the same drift.

A **parametrization** is a rule for how three things scale with width (the hidden size, such as `d_model`): each layer's initialization variance, any constant multiplier applied to a layer's output, and each layer's learning rate. The **standard parametrization (SP)** is what PyTorch does by default: initialization variance proportional to 1/fan_in for every layer and one global learning rate.

**Maximal Update Parametrization (muP)** is a different rule. Under it, many optimal HPs stay roughly fixed as width grows, so they can be tuned on a small model and copied.

The paper explains the idea with a toy problem. Draw $n$ independent numbers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with mean 0 and variance 1, scale their sum by a knob $c$, and pay a loss that depends on the result. By the central limit theorem the sum has spread $\sqrt{n}$, so the best $c$ must shrink like $1/\sqrt{n}$. If instead you tune $\alpha = c\sqrt{n}$, the best $\alpha$ does not depend on $n$ at all.

To make this concrete, pick the loss $f(z) = (z^2-1)^2$. With $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, c^2 n)$ the expected loss works out exactly:

blocks.caption: Our concrete instance of the paper's Section 2 example. The minimum loss is 2/3 at every n.

blocks.title: Same problem, two ways to turn the knob

scenes.caption: n = 256. Both curves reach the same minimum loss of 2/3. The best c is at log2 c = -4.79 (c = 0.0361); the best alpha is at log2 alpha = -0.79 (alpha = 0.577).
n = 1024. The c curve slides left by exactly one unit (best log2 c = -5.79) because every 4x in n halves the best c. The alpha curve does not move.
n = 4096. Best log2 c is now -6.79. The c that was optimal at n = 256 now gives loss 75.7 instead of 0.667. The alpha curve is still identical.
n = 16384. Best log2 c = -7.79 and the old c gives loss 1323.7. Tuning alpha once at any n would have been enough.

blocks.prompt: You tuned c on the n = 256 problem and found c* = 0.0361. You copy that c to the n = 4096 problem. Using the formula above, roughly what loss do you get, compared with the best possible 0.667?
blocks.reveal:
Plug c = 0.0361 and n = 4096 into $3c^4n^2 - 2c^2n + 1$: the loss is about **75.7**, more than 100 times the optimum. Copying $\alpha^* = 0.577$ instead gives exactly 0.667 at every n.

This is the paper's whole argument in miniature: SP is like tuning c, muP is like tuning alpha. The fix is not a better guess of the new c, it is choosing a knob whose optimum does not move.

blocks.md: In a real network the "knob" is not one number. Learning rate, initialization variance and output multipliers all interact, and each layer type needs its own width scaling. The paper stresses that reparametrizing only the learning rate is not enough: in its Transformer sweep, wide SP models still did worse than same-width muP models even after their learning rate was tuned.

blocks.title: muTransfer: tune small, copy to large

nodes.label:

scale, multipliers

Train the target
once, no sweep

scenes.caption: Step 1: write the model you actually want in muP. Nothing is trained yet.
Step 2: build a proxy by shrinking width (and optionally depth). It runs the same code with smaller dimensions, so it fits on one GPU.
Step 3: tune HPs on the proxy with any search method. Each trial is cheap, and trials run in parallel on separate GPUs.
Step 4: copy the HPs unchanged into the full-width muP model and train it once. The paper calls this zero-shot transfer.
Copying the same numbers into an SP model is naive transfer. In the paper's IWSLT, WMT and BERT experiments that training diverged.

blocks.md: muTransfer has three steps: parametrize the target in muP, tune a smaller version of it, copy the tuned HPs to the target. It works because muP makes the optimal HPs converge to fixed values as width grows.

muP is not a formula that predicts the best SP learning rate for a bigger model. It changes how every layer's init and update scale with width, so a wide muP model trains differently from (and in the paper's experiments, better than) a wide SP model.

blocks.question: In the toy problem, what is the best value of the knob c when n = 4096?
options: 0.0361, the same as at n = 256
blocks.explain: $c^* = 1/\sqrt{3n} = 1/\sqrt{12288} \approx 0.00902$. The c knob shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so 16x the width gives a 4x smaller c. 0.577 is the best alpha, which is the width-independent knob.

blocks.question: A colleague says: "We don't need muP, we will just tune the global learning rate again at every width in SP." What does the Tensor Programs V evidence say about this plan?
options: It is equivalent to muP, only slower
It costs a full sweep per size, and even with the best global LR the wide SP model can underperform the same-width muP model
It always diverges at large width
It works, because the best learning rate in SP does not depend on width
blocks.explain: Retuning per size is expensive, and in the paper's Figure 1 the width-8192 SP Transformer was worse than the width-8192 muP model even after LR tuning. One global LR cannot fix the fact that different layers in SP update at different speeds as width grows.

lessons.title: What breaks in SP after a single training step

blocks.md:
muP is built from three goals, quoted in the `mup` README. At any time during training: 1. every (pre)activation vector has coordinates of size $\Theta(1)$, 2. the network output is $O(1)$, 3. every parameter is updated as much as possible (in its width scaling) without divergence.

$\Theta(1)$ means the typical coordinate size stays the same order as width $n$ grows; it neither blows up nor shrinks to zero. SP satisfies goal 1 at initialization, which is why it looks fine. The trouble starts after the first update.

Everything hinges on one fact about a matrix $A$ times a vector $v$, both with entries of size about 1:

- If $A$ has independent random entries (like a freshly initialized weight), each entry of $Av$ is a sum of $n$ terms with random signs, so it has size about $\sqrt{n}$ (central limit theorem).
- If $A$ is an outer product built from $v$ itself, like a gradient update $\Delta W = u\,v^\top$ that was computed from the very input it will multiply, each entry of $Av$ is $u_i (v^\top v)$, and $v^\top v$ is a sum of $n$ positive terms of size 1, so it is about $n$ (law of large numbers).

blocks.title: Entry size of Av: random A versus update-like A

scenes.caption: We measure the mean absolute entry of Av at four widths (one random draw each, computed with NumPy). First, the reference columns.
Random A: entries are 6.2, 13.9, 25.3, 52.3. Each is about 0.8 x sqrt(n) (0.8 is the mean absolute value of a unit Gaussian). Growth is like sqrt(n).
Update-like A = u v^T: entries are 44.3, 232.1, 797.3, 3393.2, about 0.8 x n. Growth is like n, so an update needs a 1/n factor where an init needs only 1/sqrt(n).

blocks.md:
This explains why one rule cannot serve both initialization and updates. Initialization with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}$ (standard deviation $1/\sqrt{n}$) cancels the $\sqrt{n}$ growth of random weights. But an update $\Delta W$ is aligned with the activations it multiplies, so $\Delta W\,x$ grows like $n$ times the entry size of $\Delta W$.

Adam makes this concrete. Adam divides each gradient entry by its own running scale, so every entry of $\Delta W$ is roughly $\pm\eta$ no matter how wide the layer is. Then the entries of $\Delta W\,x$ are about $\eta n$. To keep them $\Theta(1)$, a hidden layer's Adam learning rate must scale like $1/\text{fan\_in}$.

The paper's smallest example shows SP failing. Take a linear network with scalar input and output, $f(x) = V^\top U x$, with $U, V \in \mathbb{R}^n$. In SP, $U_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and $V_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1/n)$, so $f$ is order 1 at init. One SGD step with learning rate 1 gives $V' = V + \theta U$ and $U' = U + \theta V$ for some order-1 scalar $\theta$ that depends on the data and loss:

blocks.tex: f'(x) = (V^\top U + \theta\, U^\top U + \theta\, V^\top V + \theta^2\, U^\top V)\,x
blocks.caption: Equation 5 of Tensor Programs V. The term $\theta U^\top U$ is a sum of n squares, so it grows like n.

blocks.prompt: Now switch to muP for this network: $V_\alpha \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/n^2)$, learning rate $1/n$ for $V$ and $n$ for $U$. After one step $f'/x = V^\top U + \theta n^{-1} U^\top U + \theta n V^\top V + \theta^2 U^\top V$. With $\theta = 1$, what value does it approach as $n$ grows?
blocks.reveal: About **2**. $n^{-1} U^\top U \approx 1$ and $n V^\top V \approx n \cdot n \cdot (1/n^2) = 1$, while $V^\top U$ and $U^\top V$ shrink toward 0. The simulation in the next figure gives 1.97, 1.98, 2.00, 2.00 at widths 64 to 4096. Both layers moved by an order-1 amount, and nothing blew up.

blocks.title: Output of f(x) = V^T U x before and after one SGD step

scenes.caption: SP at init: mean |f/x| over 200 seeds is about 0.8 at every width. Initialization looks healthy. (The bar scale resets in each scene.)
SP after one step with theta = 1: f/x averages 63.8, 256.1, 1019.6, 4089.2. That is about n + 1, because theta U^T U grows like n. Wider is worse.
muP at init: |f/x| is 0.10, 0.053, 0.025, 0.012. It shrinks like 1/sqrt(n) because V has variance 1/n^2. This is expected and harmless.
muP after one step: f/x is 1.97, 1.98, 2.00, 2.00. Both U and V contributed an order-1 change, and the result is the same at every width.

blocks.md:
The same imbalance appears in real Transformers trained with Adam. The paper's Figure 5 tracks how far values move from their initial values over 4 Adam steps. In SP, the output logits and the attention logits change by amounts that grow with width, while the word embeddings change by a width-independent amount.

So shrinking the global learning rate to tame the logits makes the embeddings effectively stop learning in wide models. Some layers update too fast, others too slow, and no single learning rate fixes both. muP gives each layer type its own width scaling so that all hidden activations update at the same speed.

Common misconception: "SP is broken only because the learning rate is too large for big models." Lowering it uniformly fixes the exploding layers but freezes others, such as the input embeddings. The issue is the *relative* scaling between layers.

Random weights times activations grow like sqrt(n); updates times activations grow like n, because updates are correlated with the activations they act on. muP sets each layer's init and learning rate so that both effects stay order 1.

blocks.question: You train a hidden d x d layer with Adam. You widen d from 1024 to 4096 and want the per-coordinate change of $\Delta W\,x$ after one step to stay the same. What should the layer's learning rate do?
options: Stay the same, because Adam already normalizes gradients
Be divided by 2, the square root of the width ratio
Be divided by 4, the width ratio
Be multiplied by 4
blocks.explain: Adam makes each entry of $\Delta W$ about $\pm\eta$ regardless of width, and $\Delta W$ is aligned with $x$, so $\Delta W\,x$ entries scale like $\eta \cdot \text{fan\_in}$. Keeping them fixed when fan_in grows 4x means dividing $\eta$ by 4. The square-root rule would be right for random, uncorrelated matrices, not for updates.

blocks.question: In the SP perceptron $f = V^\top U x$, which term in $f'$ is responsible for the blow-up after one step?
options: $V^\top U$, the initial output
$\theta\, V^\top V$
$\theta\, U^\top U$
$\theta^2\, U^\top V$
blocks.explain: $U$ has unit-variance entries, so $U^\top U$ is a sum of n squares of size 1, about n. $V^\top V$ is about 1 because V has variance 1/n, and the cross terms average out. The blow-up comes from the output layer's update $\theta U$, whose entries are order 1 while V was initialized at order $1/\sqrt{n}$. The input-side update $\theta V$ is tiny, which is the paper's point that SP's input layer learns too slowly.

lessons.title: The muP rules, layer by layer

blocks.md:
To apply muP you first sort every dimension into **infinite** (grows with width: `d_model`, `d_ffn`, `d_head`, `n_head`) or **finite** (fixed: vocabulary size, context length, input pixels). Then sort every parameter tensor by how many infinite dimensions it has:

- **Matrix-like** (two infinite dims): hidden weights such as the Q, K, V, O projections and the MLP matrices.
- **Vector-like** (one infinite dim): input weights such as the token embedding, output weights such as the unembedding, all biases, and LayerNorm gains.
- **Scalar-like** (none): hold their init, multiplier and learning rate constant with width.
Tensor Programs V, Table 3, gives the rules for Adam (SP in parentheses where it differs). Here fan_in is the input dimension of the weight; for a bias it is 1.

blocks.tex: \begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{input wts, biases} & \text{output wts} & \text{hidden wts} \\ \hline \text{init var} & 1/\text{fan\_in} & 1/\text{fan\_in}^2\ (1/\text{fan\_in}) & 1/\text{fan\_in} \\ \text{Adam LR} & \eta & \eta/\text{fan\_in}\ (\eta) & \eta/\text{fan\_in}\ (\eta) \end{array}
blocks.caption: Width scaling only; in practice each entry gets a tunable constant. For SGD the table differs (input LR scales with fan_out, hidden LR is constant).

blocks.md:
Two more rules complete muP for Transformers.

1. **Attention uses $q^\top k / d$ instead of $q^\top k/\sqrt{d}$**, where $d$ is the head dimension. At init q and k are independent, so $q^\top k$ grows like $\sqrt{d}$. During training they become correlated, so by the law of large numbers $q^\top k$ grows like $d$.
2. **Output weights can use an equivalent form** (the paper's Table 8): init variance constant, a forward multiplier of $1/\text{fan\_in}$ on the logits, and a constant Adam LR. This lets the output layer share weights with the input embedding, and it is what the `mup` package implements as `MuReadout`.

In practice you choose a **base width** $n_0$ (often the proxy's width) and scale by the width multiplier $m = n/n_0$. At $n = n_0$ every width factor is 1, so init, multipliers and learning rates match an SP model (only the attention scale differs, see below). As $n$ grows: hidden-weight init variance is divided by $m$, hidden-weight Adam LR is divided by $m$, the output logits are multiplied by $1/m$, and the embedding and other vector-like parameters keep their learning rate. The `mup` README writes the attention scale as `8/d` so it equals $1/\sqrt{d}$ at the common head size $d = 64$ (8/64 = 0.125).

blocks.title: Which rule applies to which Transformer parameter

nodes.label:
Q, K, V, O
d_model to d_model

MLP up and down
d_model, d_ffn

scenes.caption: Classify first. Q, K, V, O and the MLP matrices map width to width: matrix-like. Embedding, unembedding, LayerNorm gains and biases have one width dimension: vector-like.
Adam learning rates for a proxy of width 256 tuned to eta = 6e-3, scaled to width 4096 (m = 16). Only matrix-like weights get eta/m = 3.75e-4.
Init: hidden weights get variance divided by m, so std 0.08 / sqrt(16) = 0.02. The embedding keeps std 0.08. The unembedding output is multiplied by 1/m = 0.0625 in the forward pass.
Attention: logits use q.k / d instead of q.k / sqrt(d). With d_head = 128 that is a scale of 0.0078 instead of 0.088.
Optional but recommended (Appendix D.2): zero-init the unembedding and the query projection, so the proxy and the target start from the same function (output 0, attention logits 0).

blocks.title: Worked example: from a 256-wide proxy to a 4096-wide target
blocks.code:
base_width, width = 256, 4096
eta, sigma, m_emb = 6e-3, 0.08, 10.0  # tuned on proxy
wd = 0.1
m = width / base_width
hidden_lr = eta / m
hidden_std = sigma / m ** 0.5
out_mult = 1.0 / m
emb_lr, emb_std = eta, sigma
d_head = 128
attn_scale = 1.0 / d_head
hidden_wd = wd * m
print(hidden_lr * hidden_wd, eta * wd)

scenes.caption: These three values are the ones Cerebras-GPT found with a random search on its 40M-parameter muP proxy (d_model 256). We reuse them as inputs.
The width multiplier is the only new number the target needs: 4096 / 256 = 16.
Matrix-like weights: Adam LR 6e-3 / 16 = 3.75e-4 and init std 0.08 / 4 = 0.02 (variance divided by 16).
Output logits are multiplied by 1/16. Embeddings keep the tuned LR and std, and m_emb still multiplies the embedding output unchanged.
Attention scale 1/128 = 0.0078125 (SP would use 1/sqrt(128) = 0.0884).
mup's MuAdamW (default decoupled_wd=False) multiplies hidden weight decay by m, so lr x wd, the per-step shrink in PyTorch AdamW, stays 6e-4.

blocks.prompt: Same tuned values, but now the target is 8192 wide. What is the hidden-weight Adam LR, and what happens to the embedding LR?
blocks.reveal: $m = 8192/256 = 32$, so the hidden LR is $6\times10^{-3}/32 = 1.875\times10^{-4}$, the hidden init std is $0.08/\sqrt{32} \approx 0.0141$, and the logit multiplier is $1/32$. The embedding LR stays $6\times10^{-3}$: vector-like parameters do not get the $1/m$ factor under Adam in this formulation.

blocks.md: Zero-initializing the output layer and the query projection (Appendix D.2) removes a width-dependent mismatch at init: a muP network starts close to a random function whose variance shrinks with width, so a narrow proxy starts from a noisier function than the wide target. Starting both at zero output lines them up.

Every piece is needed. Keeping $1/\sqrt{d}$ attention, using plain `torch.optim.Adam` instead of `MuAdam`, or forgetting to scale `d_ffn` along with `d_model` silently breaks transfer while the model still trains. Lesson 5 shows how to catch this.

blocks.question: Which of these is a vector-like parameter in a Transformer whose width is d_model?
options: The query projection W_q (d_model x d_model)
A LayerNorm gain vector of length d_model
The MLP up-projection (d_model x 4 d_model)
A scalar temperature applied to the logits
blocks.explain: A LayerNorm gain has exactly one dimension that grows with width, so it is vector-like and keeps a constant Adam LR. W_q and the MLP matrices have two infinite dimensions (matrix-like). A scalar has none, so it is scalar-like and held constant.

blocks.question: Your model ties the input embedding and output unembedding weights. Which muP formulation from the paper fits best?
options: Table 3, because it is the main table
Table 8, which gives input and output weights the same init and LR scaling and puts a 1/fan_in multiplier on the logits
Neither; muP cannot be used with tied embeddings
SP with a smaller global learning rate
blocks.explain: Table 3 initializes output weights with variance $1/\text{fan\_in}^2$ but input weights with $1/\text{fan\_in}$, which conflicts if they are the same tensor. Table 8 is an equivalent formulation where all vector-like parameters share one rule and the width factor moves into a forward multiplier, so tying works. `MuSharedReadout` implements this.

lessons.title: muTransfer in practice: what transfers and what it saved

blocks.md:
Not every HP should transfer. The paper sorts them into three groups (its Table 1):

- **Transferable**: optimization HPs (learning rate, momentum, Adam betas, LR schedule), initialization scales and parameter multipliers, including per-layer versions.
- **Not transferable**: regularization HPs such as dropout and weight decay. How much regularization you need depends on model size and data size together, and muP only accounts for model size.
- **Transferred across**: width (with theory behind it), plus depth, batch size, training time and sequence length (validated empirically on Transformers only).

Transfer has caveats. In the paper's Transformer experiments, HPs transferred once the proxy met some minimums (examples given: width 256, depth 4, batch size 32, sequence length 128, 5000 training steps) and the target stayed in a reasonable range. Depth transfer worked only for pre-LayerNorm Transformers, and the best init std did not transfer well across depth, so the authors fixed it while tuning other HPs. The exact optimum can shift slightly with scale, but the loss cost of that shift was much smaller than in SP.

**BERT.** The authors tuned a roughly 13M-parameter proxy (shrunk in width and depth) by sampling 256 HP combinations and trained each for $10^5$ steps. The total tuning compute was about the same as one full BERT-large pretraining. One proxy served both BERT-base and BERT-large. Naive transfer (the same HPs in SP) diverged for both.

blocks.title: BERT pretraining test loss (lower is better)

scenes.caption: BERT-base: muTransfer from the 13M proxy reached test loss 1.970 against 1.995 for the published Megatron HPs (Table 6).
BERT-large: 1.683 against 1.731, with MNLI 87.0/86.5 vs 86.3/86.2. No HP was ever tuned on BERT-large itself.

blocks.md:
**GPT-3 6.7B.** The target had 32 blocks of width 4096. The proxy kept the depth and shrank width to 256, about 40M parameters, which the paper describes as 168 times smaller. A random search on the proxy tuned learning rate, init scale, attention and output temperatures, and embedding multipliers. Tuning cost was 7% of the pretraining cost. The resulting model beat the published 6.7B GPT-3 and was comparable to the 13B model on the paper's evaluation suite.

Read the caveats too: the re-run baseline mistakenly used absolute attention while the muP model used relative attention, and the muP model was trained in FP32 because of numerical divergences, while the baselines used FP16.

**Cerebras-GPT** (2023) is an independent use. It tuned a 40M-parameter muP proxy (d_model 256, 32 layers) with a 200-sample random search on 600M tokens and got $\eta = 6\times10^{-3}$, $\sigma = 0.08$, embedding multiplier 10. It reused them for models from 111M to 2.7B parameters with no other changes.

blocks.title: Cerebras-GPT: how far each model lands from the scaling-law fit

scenes.caption: Standard deviation of each model's Pile loss around the SP scaling-law fit: 0.66% for SP models. That is larger than the 0.35% run-to-run noise from seeds alone.
muP models deviated by only 0.04%, about 16x less, and averaged 0.43% better loss than the SP fit. Predictable models make scaling-law extrapolation more reliable.

blocks.code:
import torch.nn as nn
from mup import MuReadout, set_base_shapes, MuAdamW

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width, d_in=32, d_out=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.inp = nn.Linear(d_in, width)
        self.hid = nn.Linear(width, width)
        self.out = MuReadout(width, d_out, readout_zero_init=True)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.out(self.hid(self.inp(x).relu()).relu())

base = Net(width=256)    # shapes only, never trained
delta = Net(width=512)   # tells mup which dims scale
model = Net(width=4096)
set_base_shapes(model, base, delta=delta)  # before optimizer creation
opt = MuAdamW(model.parameters(), lr=6e-3)  # hidden groups get lr / 16
blocks.caption: Minimal use of the microsoft/mup package, following its README. At width 256 this model is identical to SP; at 4096 the readout is scaled by 1/16 and the hidden weight's LR is divided by 16.

blocks.md: Reverse muTransfer (Appendix I): take the HPs of an unstable large run, apply them to a small muP model, and reproduce the instability cheaply. The authors traced a width-8192 divergence to exploding attention logits this way, and reproduced a 6B model's blow-ups on a 100M model.

Don't expect dropout or weight decay tuned on a small proxy to be optimal for a much larger model trained on different amounts of data. The paper also notes that muTransfer may not be enough for fine-tuning on small datasets, where regularization matters most.

blocks.question: You tuned a muP proxy and want to copy its HPs to the target. Which HP is the paper's Table 1 least confident will transfer?
options: The learning rate schedule shape
The output-layer multiplier
The dropout rate
The Adam beta2
blocks.explain: Dropout is a regularization HP. The right amount depends on model size and dataset size together, and muP only reparametrizes model size. Schedules, multipliers and Adam betas are optimization or parametrization HPs, which the paper lists as transferable.

blocks.question: A team tunes a width-256 muP proxy, then launches the 4096-wide target with the same HPs but builds it with plain `nn.Linear` output and `torch.optim.AdamW`. What should they expect?
options: Identical results, since the HPs are the same
Better results, since SP is more flexible
Behaviour like naive SP transfer: logits that grow with width and a learning rate that is too large for hidden layers, often divergence
Slower but stable training
blocks.explain: The tuned numbers only mean something inside muP. Without the 1/m logit multiplier and the 1/m hidden Adam LR, the target is an SP model with a proxy-sized learning rate, which is exactly the naive transfer that diverged in the paper's IWSLT, WMT and BERT experiments.

lessons.title: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops

blocks.md:
muP is easy to get subtly wrong, and a wrong implementation still trains. The paper's answer is the **coordinate check**, which plays the role gradient checking plays for autograd: for several widths, train for a few steps and record the average coordinate size of every activation vector. The README uses `l1 = x.abs().mean()`.

If muP is implemented correctly the curves are flat across width. If some activation grows or shrinks with width after a step or two, something is mis-scaled. The README suggests using a learning rate larger than in real training, so that any exploding coordinates show up quickly.

blocks.title: A coordinate check, step by step

scenes.caption: Simplified sketch (the mup package's get_coord_data does this for every module). Build a model and its optimizer at one width.
t = 0 is initialization, before any update. Record the mean absolute value of the second hidden pre-activation.
Take one optimizer step, then measure again at t = 1.
Repeat at the widest model. Compare l1 at t = 1 across widths: SP gives 10.775 at width 4096, muP gives 0.605.

blocks.title: Coord check: mean |h2| across widths, SP vs muP

scenes.caption: Our NumPy run (simplified: 2-hidden-layer ReLU MLP, input 32, output 10, batch 64, MSE, Adam lr 0.01, base width 128, 3 seeds). At init both are flat near 0.55.
SP after 1 Adam step: 0.59, 0.83, 1.38, 2.67, 5.27, 10.78. Doubling width roughly doubles it, the Adam update effect from lesson 2. The bar scale resets per scene.
muP after 1 Adam step: 0.592 to 0.609 at every width. Flat curves are the sign of a correct implementation.
muP after 3 steps: still flat, 0.640 to 0.670. In SP after 3 steps the width-4096 value has reached 18.36.

blocks.prompt: In the same muP run, the network *output* at init has mean |o| of 0.366, 0.327, 0.199, 0.156, 0.102, 0.074 from width 128 to 4096. Does that mean the implementation is broken?
blocks.reveal: No. The README lists two quantities that are expected to shrink at init in muP, at a $1/\sqrt{\text{width}}$ rate: the network output and the attention logits. They are transient: after one step our output values were 0.47 to 0.53 at every width. Zero-initializing the readout (`readout_zero_init=True`) and the query projection removes the discrepancy entirely. Growth after a few steps, or shrinking that persists, would indicate a bug.

blocks.md: A second cheap check is **wider is better**. In muP, with HPs held fixed, a wider model should reach equal or lower training loss at every point in training. The paper stress-tested this on a 4-layer GPT-3-style model from width 256 to 32,768. In SP the pattern can break: wider models start doing worse past some width. If a wider muP model does worse early in training, suspect the implementation first.

Practical pitfalls listed in the `mup` README:

- Call `set_base_shapes` before any custom re-initialization and before creating the optimizer, and use `mup.init` functions for custom init.
- The delta model must differ in every dimension you scale (for example `d_ffn` as well as `d_model`).
- `torch.nn.DataParallel` drops the `infshape` attributes mup attaches; use `DistributedDataParallel`.
- `torch.save` does not keep `infshape`. After loading, call `set_base_shapes(..., rescale_params=False)`.
- Custom schedulers must change `lr` relatively (`pg['lr'] *= 2`), never absolutely, or the per-group width scaling is erased.

muP has known edges. Its theory covers width. Depth transfer in Tensor Programs V is empirical and was seen only in pre-LN Transformers. Tensor Programs VI (Depth-muP) derived a depth scaling for residual networks whose blocks have one layer, and reported fundamental limitations when each block is deeper, as in modern Transformers.

A later paper by Yang, Simon and Bernstein gives a compact way to remember the width rule: scale the spectral norm of each weight matrix and of its updates like $\sqrt{\text{fan\_out}/\text{fan\_in}}$. That one condition yields an elementary derivation of muP.

Before trusting muTransfer, run a coord check over a wide range of widths with a large learning rate. Flat curves after a few steps (apart from the output and attention logits at init) mean the parametrization is right.

blocks.question: A coord check of your muP Transformer shows the attention logits growing roughly like the square root of width after two steps, while every other curve is flat. What is the most likely bug?
options: The base width is too small
Attention still divides q.k by sqrt(d_head) instead of d_head
Weight decay is not scaled
The learning rate is too small for a coord check
blocks.explain: Once q and k become correlated during training, $q^\top k$ grows like $d$, so a $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale leaves logits growing like $\sqrt{d}$ times their target size as heads widen, while the rest of the network is fine. Switching to $1/d$ (or 8/d as in the README) fixes it.

blocks.question: Your training loop sets the learning rate with `for pg in opt.param_groups: pg['lr'] = base_lr * warmup(step)`, using a MuAdamW optimizer. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; MuAdamW recomputes width scaling every step
Every group, including the hidden-weight groups, gets the same learning rate, so the 1/m width scaling is lost and the model behaves like SP
Only the embedding learning rate changes
Training becomes deterministic
blocks.explain: MuAdamW encodes muP by splitting parameters into groups whose `lr` was already divided by the width multiplier. Assigning an absolute value overwrites that. The README's rule is to set lr relative to the group's current value (`pg['lr'] *= 2`); for warmup, store each group's initial lr and multiply it by the warmup factor.
